label: Overview
title: A calmer way to check on your money.
lead: Ledgr is a responsive personal-finance dashboard MVP. It brings balance, spending, income, budgets and savings goals into one quiet view, and turns raw numbers into plain-language answers.

items.label: My role
items.title: UI/UX designer
items.text: Product framing, information architecture, UI, design system, interaction and motion design, working prototype.

items.label: Platform
items.title: Responsive web
items.text: Desktop 12-column grid, tablet 6-column, phone single column with a floating tab bar.

items.label: Scope
items.title: MVP · 4 core screens
items.text: Overview, Transactions, Budgets, Goals, plus quick-add flows, light & dark themes and a guided tour.

items.label: Prototype
items.title: Fully interactive
items.text: Built in React + TypeScript, set in Plus Jakarta Sans; 3D guided tour with Three.js & GSAP.

a.label: The challenge
a.text: Finance apps show everything, so people understand nothing, and opening them becomes a source of anxiety.

b.label: The outcome
b.text: One hero number, honest comparisons, insights in plain language, and every key action within one tap.

label: The problem
title: “Am I okay this month?”
lead: That’s the real question behind almost every visit to a finance app. Most dashboards answer it with a wall of charts. I framed four friction points to design against:

items.title: Information overload
items.text: Every widget competes for attention, so the single number people care about gets lost.

items.title: Unfair comparisons
items.text: Mid-month, half a month is compared with all of last month, so users always look like they’re overspending.

items.title: Hidden leaks
items.text: New subscriptions and recurring charges slip through unnoticed until they add up.

items.title: Logging feels like a chore
items.text: Manual entry is slow and fiddly, so people stop keeping their picture up to date.

label: Who it’s for
title: Designed for the busy, not the obsessive.
lead: Ledgr isn’t for spreadsheet power users. It’s for people who want a quick, reassuring check-in, and a nudge only when something needs attention.

cols.title: Goals
items: Know at a glance if the month is on track
Save steadily for a few clear goals

blocks.label: Job to be done
blocks.text: When I open my finance app, I want to know straight away whether I’m on track, so I can either relax or adjust before it’s too late.

blocks.title: How might we…
items: …answer “am I okay?” in under five seconds?

label: Design principles
title: Five rules every screen had to follow.
lead: These principles turned the problem framing into concrete UI decisions, and settled debates whenever a new widget wanted attention.

items.title: One hero number
items.text: The total balance is the only oversized figure on the screen, and the cents are softened. Your eye reads “$115K” first, then the details: a clear answer before any analysis.

items.title: Colour has a job
items.text: Lime is reserved for celebration: the savings goal closest to completion, active navigation and the primary shortcut. Spending it anywhere else would dilute the reward.

items.title: Honest data is good UX
items.text: Mid-month comparisons use the same day of last month, never a half month against a full one. Category colours keep a fixed order, so a category’s colour never changes when filters do.

items.title: Say it, don’t chart it
items.text: Ledgr finds the category that moved most and states it in one sentence. Past a +200% change it switches from a percentage to a dollar amount, because “+1,700%” means nothing to anyone.

items.title: Protect the moment
items.text: New recurring charges are pulled to the top of the activity list for a one-tap decision. That’s the moment the app actually saves someone money.

label: Information architecture
title: Four destinations. One-tap actions everywhere.
lead: A flat structure keeps every screen within one tap. High-frequency actions (add a transaction, fund a goal, switch currency or theme) are global, not buried in pages.

label: Layout & hierarchy
title: Read it top-left to bottom-right, like a story.
lead: A 12-column grid gives every card a role: Know where you stand, Celebrate progress, Understand what changed, Act on it, then Plan ahead.

items.title: 12 → 6 → 1 columns
items.text: Desktop, tablet and phone layouts reuse the same cards, with spans changing per breakpoint.

items.title: 28 px radius, 20 px gutters
items.text: Generous, consistent rhythm keeps a dense dashboard feeling calm.

items.title: Card anatomy
items.text: Icon chip, title, one action. Every card has the same header, so it scans in a second.

label: Colour
title: Warm neutrals, one confident accent.
lead: All colour is defined as role-based tokens, so light and dark themes switch in one place, and data colours never get borrowed for UI chrome.

items.title: Data visualisation · fixed order
items.text: Housing, Food & dining, Transport, Shopping, Entertainment, Other. Validated for colour-vision deficiency as adjacent pairs, separately for light and dark surfaces. A neutral “Other” keeps the donut’s first and last colours apart.

items.title: Status · always icon + label
items.text: On track, Near limit and Over budget never rely on colour alone.

items.title: Dark theme · hand-tuned, not inverted
items.text: Surfaces #0C0D0B and #17191B, and lime becomes the primary action.

label: Type & components
title: Plus Jakarta Sans, all the way down.
lead: A geometric sans that feels modern and precise for numbers, with warmth in its curves. Large figures use proportional digits; columns use tabular figures so they line up.

label: Key screen · Overview
title: Everything that matters, nothing that doesn’t.
lead: Balance, progress, spending, income, activity, cash flow, budgets and accounts on one page, each card answering exactly one question.

blocks.alt: Ledgr overview dashboard on desktop and phone

label: Understanding spending
title: Explore when you want. Get the answer when you don’t.
lead: Charts are there for people who want to dig in, with hover read-outs and a table view, but the headline is always written in plain language.

items.title: Hover to focus
items.text: Hovering a category dims the rest and turns the centre of the donut into a read-out.

items.title: Fair deltas
items.text: “↑ 17.1% vs same day in Sep”: comparisons always say what they’re compared with.

items.title: Tooltips with the net
items.text: Each month shows in, out and the net result, colour-coded and labelled.

items.title: Chart ⇄ table
items.text: One toggle swaps the chart for an accessible table with exact values.

label: Log a transaction
title: From “Add” to updated dashboard in seconds.
lead: A big amount field first, because that’s what people remember. Then payee, then one-tap category chips. Clear errors, and smart defaults for account and date.

items: Open. Expense is pre-selected and the amount field leads the form.
Fill. Category chips with icons are faster than a dropdown.
Done. It appears in Activity, and balance, spending and budgets all recalculate.

blocks.label: Errors that help
blocks.text: Validation runs on save, not while typing. Messages say what to do (“Enter an amount greater than zero”) and appear in a calm, tinted banner instead of a wall of red.

label: Budgets & goals
title: Plan ahead without the guilt trip.
lead: Budgets show pace, status and what’s left per day. Goals turn savings into progress you can see, with the exact monthly amount needed to finish on time.

a.label: Budgets · from the prototype
a.text: $3,277 of $4,140 spent, with $863 left: about $62 a day for the 14 days remaining.

b.label: Goals · from the prototype
b.text: $34,792 saved toward $88,400 across 4 goals, with one-tap amounts to fund a goal.

label: Dark mode
title: Calm by day, beautiful by night.
lead: A hand-tuned dark theme, not an inverted one. Surfaces step up in lightness for depth, chart colours are re-validated against the dark background, and lime becomes the primary action colour.

label: Responsive
title: Built for the thumb, not shrunk for it.
lead: On phones the same cards stack into one column, navigation moves to a floating bottom tab bar, and quick-add opens as a bottom sheet within easy reach.

label: Accessibility
title: Small details that make it trustworthy.
lead: Money is personal and stressful. These details make sure Ledgr is legible, predictable and private for everyone.

items.title: Colour-blind-safe charts
items.text: Palette checked for CVD separation in both themes.

items.title: Never colour alone
items.text: Statuses pair icon, label and colour; charts have legends.

items.title: Keyboard friendly
items.text: Visible focus rings, a skip link, focus moves into dialogs and returns on close; Escape closes them.

items.title: Screen-reader labels
items.text: Icon buttons, charts and progress bars are all labelled.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: Animations are minimised when the OS asks for it.

items.title: Privacy mode
items.text: One tap masks every amount, for checking your balance in public.

label: Outcome & next steps
title: A working MVP, ready to put in front of users.
lead: Ledgr shipped as a fully interactive, responsive prototype, not just static mockups, so the next step can be real usability testing.

items.title: What I’d validate next
items: Usability test: can users answer “am I okay?” in 5 s?
Is the review queue noticed and trusted?

blocks.label: What I learned
blocks.text: Good finance UX isn’t about showing more data. It’s about removing the anxiety of reading it. Prototyping in code surfaced details (like unfair mid-month comparisons) that static mockups would have hidden.
